\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{liu2023codeexecution,chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,ding2024semcoder,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
The intuition is straightforward: more execution information should help the model make better predictions.
Yet for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), this intuition is wrong.
Complete traces \emph{actively degrade} accuracy compared to compact exception events, despite containing strictly more information.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig1_trace_overview}
\vspace{-8pt}
\caption{Overview of the verdict prediction pipeline. Source code and a test input are executed to produce a full raw trace, from which four conditions extract different representations: \texttt{no\_trace} (source code only), \texttt{full\_trace} (complete line-by-line trace), VOTA (Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction: exception events, assertion comparisons, and loop summaries), and \texttt{exception\_only} (only exception/error events). Information density decreases from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only}, yet accuracy follows the opposite direction (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}). Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_examples} provides input/output examples.}
\label{fig:trace_overview}
\end{figure*}


Prior work found trace utility to be task-dependent \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks where output noise confounds the analysis.
Verdict prediction offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, and controlled component ablation directly measures how trace content affects SFT learning.
This approach aligns with recent *ACL precedent: CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} uses execution prediction to probe code reasoning, and NExT \citep{ni2024next} uses trace-augmented chain-of-thought for program repair.

We present a systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and Mostly Basic Python Problems--sanitized (MBPP-sanitized) \citep{austin2021program}, we evaluate four models across three architecture families and 1.5B to 13B parameters: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2024coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

The central result: complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone, while compact exception events achieve near-perfect accuracy (${\geq}$99\%) across all four models, an 18--23 percentage-point (pp) gap (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
A simple regex exploiting a format marker matches this ceiling, so the interesting question is not why exceptions help but \emph{why complete traces hurt}.
Marker removal collapses the regex to near-chance while SFT retains $>$97\%; cross-dataset transfer confirms SFT acquires diagnostic patterns beyond format matching (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

Gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution; content quality at inference accounts for the majority (\S\ref{sec:density}).
Training dynamics corroborate this: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates without convergence (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
A tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp performance transition near 512 tokens, coinciding with the first appearance of structured execution markers (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

While exception events structurally encode verdict direction (exception present typically implies failure), the non-trivial finding is that providing strictly more information (complete traces containing all exception data) degrades performance by 18--23pp.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy} despite containing all diagnostic information: across four models (1.5B--13B, three families), complete traces (77--82\%) remain near source-code-only levels while compact exception events close an 18--23pp gap to ${\geq}$99.33\% (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\item \textbf{Semantic vs.\ format-marker decomposition}: marker removal collapses a format-exploiting regex by 71pp while SFT drops only 2pp; cross-dataset transfer (99.4--100\%) shows the learned signal generalizes beyond format markers (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

\item \textbf{A two-tier signal hierarchy and its mechanistic explanation}: exception/assertion signals (${\geq}$98.53\%) dominate loop compression (77--86\%) by 12+pp with non-overlapping CIs, and a sharp transition at ${\sim}$512 tail tokens yields a practical fallback (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}). Controlled gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution, assigning the majority to content quality at inference (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\end{enumerate}

3	\subsection{Task Definition and Diagnostic Signal Metrics}
4	
5	We study \emph{verdict prediction}: given a Python function, a test input, and an optional execution trace, predict whether the test passes or fails.
6	The model produces a single token (\texttt{pass} or \texttt{fail}), making this a binary classification task.
7	Unlike code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile} or output prediction \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, verdict prediction isolates the model's ability to detect faults from its ability to simulate execution, providing cleaner ablation contrasts than generation tasks.
8	
9	To quantify signal quality without circular reference to model accuracy, we define the \emph{diagnostic token ratio} $d = n_{\text{diag}} / n_{\text{total}}$, where $n_{\text{diag}}$ counts tokens matching exception or assertion patterns.
10	This model-free metric correlates with accuracy at Pearson $r{=}0.949$ ($p{=}0.014$, $N{=}5$, df=3; treat as descriptive), but captures only the \emph{explicit} diagnostic pathway; tail-truncated conditions achieve 93--98\% with $d {\approx} 0$, indicating a second, implicit signal channel operating through terminal execution state (\S\ref{sec:density}).
11	
12	\subsection{Dataset}
13	\label{sec:dataset}
14	
15	We sampled 10 candidate solutions per problem from Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (temperature 0.8, top\_p 0.95) for 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} (164) and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program} (427), executed each against canonical tests with \texttt{sys.settrace} to obtain line-level traces and pass/fail verdicts, yielding 5,910 pairs (67\% pass, 33\% fail).
16	The dataset is split 80/20 by problem ID into 4,720 training and 1,190 test samples (majority baseline: 71.51\%).
17	The \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (39.45\% train, 48.99\% test duplicates); these duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem, with the train--test split enforced at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}).
18	
19	\subsection{Trace Representations}
20	
21	We define seven conditions that vary the trace information available (Figure~\ref{fig:trace_overview}):
22	\begin{itemize}
23	\item \texttt{no\_trace}: Source code and test input only.
24	\item \texttt{full\_trace}: Complete line-by-line trace with variable states.
25	\item \texttt{VOTA} (Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction): Exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression (Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_algorithm}).
26	\item \texttt{exception\_only}: Only exception/error events.
27	\item \texttt{ae\_only}: Only assertion-point actual/expected pairs.
28	\item \texttt{loop\_only}: Only loop compression summaries.
29	\item \texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae}: VOTA without assertion-point information.
30	\end{itemize}

36	All conditions use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA; \citealp{hu2022lora}) with rank=16, $\alpha$=32, dropout=0.05 on all linear layers, 3 epochs, effective batch size 32, learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$ with linear warmup/decay, max sequence length 2{,}048 tokens.
37	Sequences exceeding this limit are truncated while preserving the verdict label.
38	The primary seed is 42; seeds 123 and 456 test \texttt{exception\_only} robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_details}).

40	\subsection{Loss Ablation}
41	
42	To probe the contribution of gradient dilution, we introduce \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only}: identical full-trace input but loss computed only on the verdict token (trace positions masked).
43	The SFTTrainer (from the TRL library) computes mean cross-entropy over label tokens, so label-only loss does not amplify the effective learning rate.

\section{Method}

\subsection{Task Definition and Diagnostic Signal Metrics}

We study \emph{verdict prediction}: given a Python function, a test input, and an optional execution trace, predict whether the test passes or fails.
The model produces a single token (\texttt{pass} or \texttt{fail}), making this a binary classification task.
Unlike code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile} or output prediction \citep{gu2024cruxeval}, verdict prediction isolates the model's ability to detect faults from its ability to simulate execution, providing cleaner ablation contrasts than generation tasks.

To quantify signal quality without circular reference to model accuracy, we define the \emph{diagnostic token ratio} $d = n_{\text{diag}} / n_{\text{total}}$, where $n_{\text{diag}}$ counts tokens matching exception or assertion patterns.
This model-free metric correlates with accuracy at Pearson $r{=}0.949$ ($p{=}0.014$, $N{=}5$, df=3; treat as descriptive), but captures only the \emph{explicit} diagnostic pathway; tail-truncated conditions achieve 93--98\% with $d {\approx} 0$, indicating a second, implicit signal channel operating through terminal execution state (\S\ref{sec:density}).

\subsection{Dataset}
\label{sec:dataset}

We sampled 10 candidate solutions per problem from Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (temperature 0.8, top\_p 0.95) for 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} (164) and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program} (427), executed each against canonical tests with \texttt{sys.settrace} to obtain line-level traces and pass/fail verdicts, yielding 5,910 pairs (67\% pass, 33\% fail).
The dataset is split 80/20 by problem ID into 4,720 training and 1,190 test samples (majority baseline: 71.51\%).
The \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions into identical rows (39.45\% train, 48.99\% test duplicates); these duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem, with the train--test split enforced at the problem level (472 train / 119 test problems, zero crossover; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}).

\subsection{Trace Representations}

We define seven conditions that vary the trace information available (Figure~\ref{fig:trace_overview}):
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{no\_trace}: Source code and test input only.
\item \texttt{full\_trace}: Complete line-by-line trace with variable states.
\item \texttt{VOTA} (Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction): Exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression (Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_algorithm}).
\item \texttt{exception\_only}: Only exception/error events.
\item \texttt{ae\_only}: Only assertion-point actual/expected pairs.
\item \texttt{loop\_only}: Only loop compression summaries.
\item \texttt{VOTA\_no\_ae}: VOTA without assertion-point information.
\end{itemize}


\subsection{Models and Training}

We evaluate four models spanning three architecture families: \textbf{Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct} \citep{qwen2024coder}, \textbf{CodeLlama-13B-Instruct} \citep{roziere2024code}, and \textbf{DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct} \citep{deepseek2024coder}, covering a 1.5B--13B parameter range (8.7$\times$).
All conditions use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA; \citealp{hu2022lora}) with rank=16, $\alpha$=32, dropout=0.05 on all linear layers, 3 epochs, effective batch size 32, learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$ with linear warmup/decay, max sequence length 2{,}048 tokens.
Sequences exceeding this limit are truncated while preserving the verdict label.
The primary seed is 42; seeds 123 and 456 test \texttt{exception\_only} robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_details}).

\subsection{Loss Ablation}

To probe the contribution of gradient dilution, we introduce \texttt{full\_trace\_label\_only}: identical full-trace input but loss computed only on the verdict token (trace positions masked).
The SFTTrainer (from the TRL library) computes mean cross-entropy over label tokens, so label-only loss does not amplify the effective learning rate.
However, this ablation simultaneously changes three variables: (1)~which tokens receive gradient updates, (2)~the implicit regularization from predicting trace tokens, and (3)~the training signal distribution.
The resulting improvement over standard \texttt{full\_trace} provides a confounded upper bound on gradient dilution's contribution.
A cleaner test (masking 99.8\% of gradient updates during \texttt{exception\_only} training) matches the diagnostic token ratio of full traces while preserving compact input, isolating gradient dilution from content quality (\S\ref{sec:density}).

1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	We evaluate across two research questions:
4	(1)~Why do complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy despite containing all diagnostic information?
5	(2)~Which trace components carry the verdict signal, and how does their density affect learning?
6	All experiments use $N{=}1{,}190$ test samples; accuracy is reported with Wilson 95\% confidence intervals (CIs).\footnote{Problem-level partition (472 train / 119 test, zero crossover; \S\ref{sec:dataset}). \texttt{exception\_only} duplicates (48.99\% test; Appendix~\ref{sec:dedup_stats}) arise from within-problem variants; deduplication yields negligible ($<$0.1pp) delta.}
7	Pairwise comparisons use paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, seed=42); all differences are significant at $p{<}.0001$ unless noted.
8	Under problem-level clustered bootstrap ($n_\text{eff}{=}119$), all cross-tier gaps remain significant ($p{<}.001$); 3 of 80 within-tier pairwise comparisons lose significance after Holm--Bonferroni correction.
9	
10	\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
11	\label{sec:cross_model}

97	Tier~1 signals are individually sufficient: \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%$\pm$0.00) exceeds VOTA (99.05\%$\pm$0.38) by +0.78pp (2/3 seeds $p{<}.05$, all directionally consistent), implying that combining signals introduces noise.

99	Individual exception subcomponents (type, stacktrace, message) each independently achieve ${\geq}$99.50\%, indicating that the binary presence of an exception event, rather than any specific subcomponent, drives Tier~1 performance (Appendix~\ref{sec:exc_subcomponent}).
100	The Tier~1/2 boundary is unambiguous: the lowest Tier~1 condition (\texttt{ae\_only} on DeepSeek, 98.53\%$\pm$0.30, 2 seeds) exceeds the highest Tier~2 (\texttt{loop\_only} on Qwen-7B, 86.05\%, CI [83.97, 87.96]) by 12.48\,pp with non-overlapping CIs (gap statistic supports $k{=}2$ clusters, silhouette ${\geq}$0.74).
101	Tier~2 \texttt{loop\_only} lifts over \texttt{no\_trace} are model-dependent: Qwen +10.92pp (7B) and +7.19pp (1.5B); DeepSeek +6.95pp; CodeLlama +0.93pp (n.s.).
102	\paragraph{Rule-based baseline comparison.}
103	The strongest non-trivial regex heuristic (B4: exception class name matching; Table~\ref{tab:regex}) achieves 93.61\% accuracy (F1=0.876), trailing SFT \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%, F1=0.997) by 6.22pp (McNemar $p{<}.001$).
104	The gap concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases: regex flags all exception events as failures, while SFT learns to distinguish caught exceptions (benign, inside \texttt{try/except}) from uncaught faults, correctly resolving 6/8 boundary samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
105	Across all formats, SFT outperforms the best applicable regex by +3.62--23.86pp (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).

107	\paragraph{Zero-shot and few-shot LLM baselines.}
108	Zero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\% across four models (42.44pp range); three-shot in-context learning on Qwen-7B (90.84\%) improves only 1.76pp.
109	SFT compresses this range to 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), closing a 6--49pp gap with 4,720 samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}).
110	\paragraph{Frontier model crossover.}
111	Two frontier models illustrate that SFT's advantage depends on input density: under \texttt{no\_trace}, GPT-4o (84.45\%) and GPT-4.1 (77.31\%) outperform SFT Qwen-7B (75.13\%), but under \texttt{exception\_only} the ranking reverses (SFT 99.83\% vs.\ GPT-4o 87.98\%).
112	Compact diagnostic input unlocks SFT's full advantage over general reasoning capacity.

114	\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
115	\label{sec:nomarker}
116	
117	The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
118	To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).
119	
120	Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
121	Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.
122	The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).
123	Regex baselines illustrate this decomposition: B5 (\texttt{[No exception data]}$\to$pass, 99.33\% with markers) collapses to 28.49\% without markers, showing it is entirely format-dependent.
124	The strongest semantic regex B4 (exception class matching, 93.61\%) is marker-invariant; SFT \texttt{nomarker} (97.65\%) exceeds it by 4.04pp, isolating the learned semantic contribution beyond pattern matching.
125	
126	\paragraph{Cross-dataset transfer.}
127	Bidirectional evaluation demonstrates generalization: HumanEval${\to}$MBPP \texttt{exception\_only} achieves 99.41\% ($N{=}4{,}270$) and MBPP${\to}$HumanEval achieves 100.0\% ($N{=}1{,}640$), while \texttt{no\_trace} drops to near-majority baseline in both directions (70.56\% vs.\ 69.02\% majority; 67.99\% vs.\ 61.65\%).
128	The near-zero transfer loss for exception signals, across independently authored problem sets with no problem overlap, shows SFT learns language-level diagnostic patterns, not dataset-specific artifacts.
129	Under marker removal, cross-dataset accuracy drops to 95.5\% ($-$3.9pp), indicating that the majority of cross-dataset transfer relies on learned diagnostic patterns rather than format markers.
130	
131	\subsection{Decomposing the Full-Trace Degradation}
132	\label{sec:density}
133	
134	The 18.07pp gap between \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) and \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) could reflect gradient dilution (diagnostic tokens are ${\sim}$1/500 of full traces, diluting gradient signal during training) or content quality (verbose input buries diagnostic signals at inference).
135	
136	\paragraph{Controlled gradient masking.}
137	To isolate gradient dilution, we mask 99.8\% of gradient updates during \texttt{exception\_only} training, matching the diagnostic token ratio of full traces while preserving compact input.
138	This yields 99.22\% (mean $-$0.61pp from \texttt{exception\_only}, 3 seeds), limiting gradient dilution to ${\leq}$4\% of the 18.07pp gap (Table~\ref{tab:density}).
139	The gradient masking bound attributes the remaining ${\geq}$96\% to content quality (diagnostic signal density at inference), though forward-pass attention during masked training is an unquantified residual.
140	Note that masking affects only the backward pass; the model still attends to all input tokens during the forward pass, so this bounds gradient dilution's contribution but does not rule out attention-based information flow as a residual confound.

166	\paragraph{Complementary evidence.}
167	Label-only loss on full traces (+4.50pp, 3 seeds) yields a confounded upper bound of ${\leq}$26\% gradient contribution, consistent with the masking estimate (${\leq}$4\%) but not significant under clustered bootstrap (95\% CI [$-$0.6, +9.8]pp).
168	Qwen-1.5B shows a similar label-only pattern (17\%/83\%, 3 seeds); CodeLlama and DeepSeek exhibit label-only collapse to majority baseline (28.5\%), limiting this complementary analysis to the Qwen family.
169	The architecture dependence suggests label-only training is sensitive to model capacity or optimization landscape; the gradient masking ablation provides a more robust, architecture-independent decomposition.
170	Cross-architecture validation on two additional families is directionally consistent (single seed each): DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B achieves 99.33\% and CodeLlama-13B achieves 100\% under 99.8\% masking, both well above the full-trace range (77--82\%, Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}), supporting content quality as the dominant factor across architectures.
171	Error analysis supports the content quality interpretation: all 217 \texttt{full\_trace} errors occur where tokenizer truncation removes diagnostic markers, manifesting through mechanical truncation rather than semantic confusion.
172	
173	\subsection{Complementary Analyses}
174	\label{sec:additional}
175	
176	\paragraph{Trace length ablation.}
177	\label{sec:trace_length}
178	Varying the head-truncated trace token budget (256--no limit) on Qwen-7B yields accuracy in a narrow 77.2\%--81.8\% band with a non-monotonic pattern: 1024-token prefixes (77.23\%) underperform 512-token prefixes (80.42\%, $p{=}.002$), because mid-length prefixes retain enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events near the trace terminus (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
179	Critically, removing the token budget entirely (no truncation) yields 81.76\%, identical to head-2048, ruling out truncation as the explanation for the full-trace degradation.
180	This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation; under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for two of three models (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model} in Appendix), with only DeepSeek showing a mild architecture-specific reversal at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048 ($-$1.5pp).
181	
182	\paragraph{Truncation direction and budget curve.}
183	Tail-truncation dramatically outperforms head-truncation: tail-2048 exceeds head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp across three models (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
184	Figure~\ref{fig:budget_curve} reveals a sharp phase transition at 384$\to$512 tail tokens: all four models simultaneously jump +13.2--22.0pp, crossing from near-baseline to 93--98\%.
185	This threshold coincides with the globals module dump boundary (${\sim}$384 tokens), beyond which structured execution markers become visible (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}).
186	Beyond 512 tokens, all 12 model$\times$seed combinations converge into [93.61\%, 98.24\%] (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}).
187	\texttt{tail\_2048} captures 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy; the residual 2--5pp gap shows semantic extraction still outperforms positional extraction.
188

193	\label{fig:budget_curve}
194	\end{figure}
195	
196	\paragraph{Calibration.}
197	\label{sec:calibration}
198	Calibration mirrors the tier hierarchy: \texttt{exception\_only} achieves ECE = 0.0027 vs.\ 0.171 for \texttt{no\_trace}, a 63$\times$ gap (Figure~\ref{fig:calibration}).
199	This calibration advantage generalizes across architectures and scales: all four models (1.5B--13B) achieve ECE ${<}$ 0.007 under \texttt{exception\_only} (Table~\ref{tab:calibration_cross} in Appendix), indicating well-calibrated predictions rather than overfit confidence.
200

205	\label{fig:calibration}
206	\end{figure}
207	
208	\paragraph{Error analysis.}
209	\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors have zero overlap with all other conditions' error sets (Jaccard = 0.000; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_overlap}); per-type breakdown shows all standard exception types achieve 100\% accuracy, with only \texttt{GeneratorExit} (a benign \texttt{BaseException} subclass) causing failures (Appendix~\ref{sec:exception_type}).
210	
211	\paragraph{Length control.}
212	Padding \texttt{exception\_only} to 2{,}048 tokens, even in a semantically loaded position (after the verdict region), yields identical accuracy (99.83\%), indicating the 18--23pp gap arises from spurious patterns in verbose trace content, not sequence length.
213	
214	\paragraph{Supplementary out-of-distribution analysis.}
215	\label{sec:debugbench}
216	On DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench} ($N{=}426$), the condition ranking is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} 100\%, VOTA 99.77\%, \texttt{no\_trace} 96.71\%.
217	However, narrow margins (3.29pp headroom from \texttt{no\_trace}) limit discriminative power; this supplementary analysis preserves the ranking but cannot establish effect sizes comparable to the primary dataset (Appendix~\ref{sec:debugbench_full}).

1	\section{Related Work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Execution Traces for Code Large Language Models (LLMs).}
4	TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} scaled trace-augmented training to 2.6M samples; \citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility task- and format-dependent, which we extend by showing that complete traces degrade SFT performance while compact exception events suffice.
5	Earlier, \citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained on execution prediction, SemCoder \citep{ding2024semcoder} introduced monologue reasoning to link code with runtime states, and \citet{dimenna2025execution} studied execution-aware models for code optimization.
6	NExT \citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} used trace chain-of-thought for repair and execution reasoning; \citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, and \citet{haque2025traces} showed trace utility for repair diminishes with complexity, both supporting our density finding.
7	CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval,xu2025cruxevalx} and LiveCodeBench \citep{jain2024livecodebench} established execution reasoning benchmarks, but none decompose which trace components contribute to classification accuracy.
8	
9	\paragraph{Verdict Prediction and Fault Localization.}
10	TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; CC2Vec \citep{hoang2020cc2vec}, APPT \citep{appt2024}, and LLM-based patch assessment \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} developed representation learning and evaluation of code changes, extending just-in-time quality assurance \citep{kamei2013large}; verdict prediction is an instance of the test oracle problem \citep{barr2015oracle,bodicoat2026oracle}.
11	Spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL; \citealp{jones2002visualization,abreu2007accuracy,wong2014dstar}) and LLM-based fault localization \citep{kang2024autofl,qin2024agentfl,shi2025farloc} share our insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal, though LLM fault localizability remains fragile under semantic-preserving mutations \citep{haroon2026faultlocalizability}.
12	TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} use selective trace extraction, and LLM repair agents \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent,xia2024agentless,bouzenia2025repairagent,wang2025openhands} increasingly leverage execution feedback, yet which trace components carry verdict signals most efficiently remains unstudied.
13	
14	\paragraph{Calibration and Data Selection.}
15	Neural network calibration \citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration,liu2025uqsurvey}, studies confidence-correctness alignment; our Expected Calibration Error (ECE) ${<}$ 0.007 suggests compact inputs improve calibration.
16	The Information Bottleneck \citep{tishby2000information}, feature selection theory \citep{guyon2003introduction}, IB-guided code fine-tuning \citep{wang2025ibft}, and LIMA \citep{zhou2023lima} predict that compressing task-irrelevant information improves learning; data pruning \citep{paul2021deep,sorscher2022beyond}, curriculum learning \citep{bengio2009curriculum}, and data-efficient code SFT \citep{lv2025dataefficient,shang2025thtb} confirm this empirically, consistent with our finding that compact exceptions converge rapidly while verbose traces oscillate.
17	Prompt compression methods \citep{jiang2023llmlingua,li2023selectivecontext} pursue a complementary goal at inference time.

\paragraph{Verdict Prediction and Fault Localization.}

1	\section{Conclusion}
2	
3	Across four code-specialized models (1.5B--13B, three families), compact exception events (${\geq}$99.33\%) outperform complete traces (77--82\%) by 18--23pp.
4	The question was never why exceptions help, but why complete traces hurt: gradient masking, cross-dataset transfer, and marker-removal robustness all point to diagnostic density rather than information quantity as the driver of SFT learning.
5	For practitioners, exception extraction should be the default preprocessing; when unavailable, tail-truncated traces (${\geq}$512 tokens) recover 93--98\%.
6	That a 7B SFT model surpasses GPT-4o by 12pp under compact input suggests that, within the ${\leq}$13B code-specialized models studied, input curation matters more than model scaling for this task; whether this holds at 30B+ or for general-purpose LLMs remains open.

\section{Conclusion}

Across four code-specialized models (1.5B--13B, three families), compact exception events (${\geq}$99.33\%) outperform complete traces (77--82\%) by 18--23pp.
The question was never why exceptions help, but why complete traces hurt: gradient masking, cross-dataset transfer, and marker-removal robustness all point to diagnostic density rather than information quantity as the driver of SFT learning.
For practitioners, exception extraction should be the default preprocessing; when unavailable, tail-truncated traces (${\geq}$512 tokens) recover 93--98\%.
That a 7B SFT model surpasses GPT-4o by 12pp under compact input suggests that, within the ${\leq}$13B code-specialized models studied, input curation matters more than model scaling for this task; whether this holds at 30B+ or for general-purpose LLMs remains open.

103	\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
104	\label{sec:vota_algorithm}
105	
106	Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.
107	
108	\begin{algorithm}[t]
109	\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
110	\label{alg:vota}
111	\small
112	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
113	\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
114	\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
115	\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
116	\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
117	\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
118	  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
119	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
120	\ENDFOR
121	\IF{no exception events found}
122	  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
123	\ENDIF
124	\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
125	\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
126	  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
127	  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
128	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
129	\ENDFOR
130	\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
131	\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
132	  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
133	    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
134	  \ENDIF
135	\ENDFOR
136	\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
137	\RETURN $V$
138	\end{algorithmic}
139	\end{algorithm}

142	\section{VOTA Trace Examples}
143	\label{sec:vota_examples}
144	
145	We provide two representative VOTA trace examples illustrating the fail and pass cases.
146	In the fail case, the exception event provides an unambiguous fault signal.
147	In the pass case, the absence of an exception event combined with a matching assertion point confirms correct execution.
148	
149	\paragraph{Fail example.}
150	A \texttt{ZeroDivisionError} triggers an \texttt{[ERROR]} event, providing a direct fault signal that is sufficient for the model to predict \texttt{fail}.
151	
152	\begin{scriptsize}
153	\begin{verbatim}
154	## Function
155	def divide(a, b):
156	    return a / b
157	
158	## Test Input
159	divide(1, 0)
160	
161	## Expected Output
162	inf
163	
164	## VOTA Trace
165	[ERROR] ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
166	
167	## Verdict
168	fail
169	\end{verbatim}
170	\end{scriptsize}
171	
172	\paragraph{Pass example.}
173	No exception is raised, and the assertion point confirms that the actual output matches the expected value.
174	
175	\begin{scriptsize}
176	\begin{verbatim}
177	## Function
178	def add(a, b):
179	    return a + b
180	
181	## Test Input
182	add(2, 3)
183	
184	## Expected Output
185	5
186	
187	## VOTA Trace
188	[No exception data in trace]
189	[ASSERT] actual=5, expected=5
190	[LOOP] No loops detected.
191	
192	## Verdict
193	pass
194	\end{verbatim}
195	\end{scriptsize}
196	
197	These examples illustrate the core asymmetry exploited by the \texttt{exception\_only} condition: fail cases produce an explicit \texttt{[ERROR]} event, while pass cases are characterized by its absence.
198	This binary signal (presence vs.\ absence of an exception) is sufficient for near-perfect verdict prediction.

254	\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
255	\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}
256	
257	DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
258	Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, consistent with complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
259	The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
260	Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
261	The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
262	The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
263	Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).
264	
265	A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
266	Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) shows that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.
267	
268	Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
269	Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).
270	
271	%% ============================================================
272	\section{Persistent Error Analysis}
273	\label{sec:irreducible}
274	
275	The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
276	Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:
277	
278	\begin{itemize}
279	\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
280	\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
281	\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
282	\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
283	\end{itemize}
284	
285	Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
286	Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
287	The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
288	This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
289	
290	Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
291	However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
292	This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
293	The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.
294

426	\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
427	Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).
428	The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
429	This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
430	Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.
431	
432	\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
433	All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), indicating that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
434	The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
435	The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).
436	
437	\paragraph{Interpretation.}
438	These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
439	The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
440	The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
441	In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
442	
443	\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
444	Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
445	Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.
446	
447	However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%), indicating that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
448	The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
449	This is consistent with the trace format: the globals module dump consumes the first ${\sim}$384 tail tokens (pure noise), so structured execution markers (\texttt{[Line~X]} variable values) only become visible when the budget exceeds this threshold.
450	
451	The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
452	The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) indicates that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

653	\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
654	\label{sec:robustness_analysis}
655	
656	The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
657	Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
658	All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.
659	VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models when excluding outlier seeds (cross-model range: 0.80pp), but DeepSeek VOTA exhibits seed-dependent instability: seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected), while seeds 123/456 (99.16\%/99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
660	This VOTA instability is confounded by tokenizer efficiency and base model differences \citep{yang2024generalization}.
661	Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
662	The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
663	The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal.

666	\section{Training Dynamics and Loss Decoupling}
667	\label{sec:training_dynamics}
668	
669	The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results are consistent across all three seeds (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen's cross-seed stability.
670	Epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in seed 42: accuracy peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), while seed 456 shows no degradation (99.33\% at both epochs).
671	Early stopping may yield marginal gains, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp).
672	The practical recommendation: for deployment, use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training loss, and train multiple seeds to select the best.
673	
674	The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, consistent with a performance limit from high trace truncation (91.7\% of samples; \S\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).
675	Seeds 123/456, which avoid the truncation-sensitive initialization basin, achieve 99.16\%/99.33\%, indicating that the deficit is seed-specific rather than a fundamental model limitation.

682	Because multiple passing solutions to the same problem produce identical (input, output) pairs in the \texttt{exception\_only} format (correct executions raise no exceptions, so the trace content is the same regardless of the solution's internal logic), the dataset contains duplicate rows.

688	Duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem (up to 10 solutions each), not from cross-problem overlap.
689	To verify that deduplication does not alter any finding, we ran a sensitivity analysis across all 19 experimental conditions (7 trace formats $\times$ 4 models, minus conditions not run): deduplication produces a negligible ($<$0.1pp) accuracy delta in every case.
690	This shows that duplicate samples neither inflate nor deflate accuracy, because duplicates share the same ground-truth label and the model's prediction is deterministic at inference time.

\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
\label{sec:vota_algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
\label{alg:vota}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\IF{no exception events found}
  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
\ENDIF
\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
\RETURN $V$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{VOTA Trace Examples}
\label{sec:vota_examples}

We provide two representative VOTA trace examples illustrating the fail and pass cases.
In the fail case, the exception event provides an unambiguous fault signal.
In the pass case, the absence of an exception event combined with a matching assertion point confirms correct execution.

\paragraph{Fail example.}
A \texttt{ZeroDivisionError} triggers an \texttt{[ERROR]} event, providing a direct fault signal that is sufficient for the model to predict \texttt{fail}.

\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
## Function
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

## Test Input
divide(1, 0)

## Expected Output
inf

## VOTA Trace
[ERROR] ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

## Verdict
fail
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize}

\paragraph{Pass example.}
No exception is raised, and the assertion point confirms that the actual output matches the expected value.

\begin{scriptsize}
\begin{verbatim}
## Function
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

## Test Input
add(2, 3)

## Expected Output
5

## VOTA Trace
[No exception data in trace]
[ASSERT] actual=5, expected=5
[LOOP] No loops detected.

## Verdict
pass
\end{verbatim}
\end{scriptsize}

These examples illustrate the core asymmetry exploited by the \texttt{exception\_only} condition: fail cases produce an explicit \texttt{[ERROR]} event, while pass cases are characterized by its absence.
This binary signal (presence vs.\ absence of an exception) is sufficient for near-perfect verdict prediction.

\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}

DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, consistent with complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).

A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) shows that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.

Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).

%% ============================================================
\section{Persistent Error Analysis}
\label{sec:irreducible}

The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
\end{itemize}

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.

Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

\paragraph{Format marker confound.}

\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}
Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).
The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.

\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), indicating that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.

However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%), indicating that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
This is consistent with the trace format: the globals module dump consumes the first ${\sim}$384 tail tokens (pure noise), so structured execution markers (\texttt{[Line~X]} variable values) only become visible when the budget exceeds this threshold.

The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) indicates that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

\section{Error Overlap Analysis}
\label{sec:error_overlap}

We analyze the overlap between error sets of different conditions to determine whether they fail on the same samples (Figure~\ref{fig:error_overlap}).

\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors (samples 901 and 905) have zero intersection with the error sets of all other conditions (Jaccard = 0.000 in all pairwise comparisons).
This orthogonality arises because \texttt{exception\_only} errors are caused by \texttt{GeneratorExit} false positives (pass samples misclassified as fail due to benign \texttt{BaseException} events), while errors from other conditions are predominantly fail samples misclassified as pass due to insufficient signal.

Among non-exception conditions, error sets exhibit hierarchical containment: \texttt{ae\_only} $\subset$ VOTA $\subset$ \texttt{loop\_only} $\subset$ \texttt{no\_trace}, with pairwise Jaccard indices increasing with signal overlap.
\texttt{loop\_only} and \texttt{full\_trace} share the highest overlap (Jaccard ${\sim}$0.65), reflecting their shared reliance on behavioral patterns rather than explicit fault indicators.

This analysis indicates that \texttt{exception\_only} operates on an independent signal dimension: its errors are representation ambiguities (iterator protocol artifacts) rather than information deficits, explaining why combining it with other signals cannot eliminate these specific errors.

The absolute margins are much narrower than on the main dataset: the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline already achieves 96.71\% (compared to 75.13\% on HumanEval+MBPP), leaving only 3.29pp of headroom for trace-based improvement.
This ceiling effect reflects a fundamental difference in fault characteristics: DebugBench bugs are synthetically injected single-point mutations, which produce code that is structurally dissimilar from the original correct solution; a model can often identify the fault from source code alone.
In contrast, the HumanEval+MBPP solutions are LLM-generated, producing natural errors (logic mistakes, edge-case failures) where the faulty and correct solutions may be structurally similar, making code-only verdict prediction substantially harder.

These results support exception-based verdict prediction as a generalizable approach: the method does not degrade on an out-of-distribution dataset, and the exception dominance ranking (exception\_only $\geq$ VOTA $>$ no\_trace) is consistent across both datasets. However, the narrow DebugBench margins are insufficient to independently validate trace importance.
The 24.70pp trace lift on the main dataset (no\_trace 75.13\% $\to$ exception\_only 99.83\%) remains the primary evidence for the value of exception-based trace signals.

\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
\label{sec:robustness_analysis}

The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.
VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models when excluding outlier seeds (cross-model range: 0.80pp), but DeepSeek VOTA exhibits seed-dependent instability: seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected), while seeds 123/456 (99.16\%/99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
This VOTA instability is confounded by tokenizer efficiency and base model differences \citep{yang2024generalization}.
Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal.

%% ============================================================
\section{Training Dynamics and Loss Decoupling}
\label{sec:training_dynamics}

The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results are consistent across all three seeds (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen's cross-seed stability.
Epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in seed 42: accuracy peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), while seed 456 shows no degradation (99.33\% at both epochs).
Early stopping may yield marginal gains, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp).
The practical recommendation: for deployment, use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training loss, and train multiple seeds to select the best.

The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, consistent with a performance limit from high trace truncation (91.7\% of samples; \S\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).
Seeds 123/456, which avoid the truncation-sensitive initialization basin, achieve 99.16\%/99.33\%, indicating that the deficit is seed-specific rather than a fundamental model limitation.

\section{Deduplication Statistics}
\label{sec:dedup_stats}

Table~\ref{tab:dedup} reports the duplication rates across trace formats.
Because multiple passing solutions to the same problem produce identical (input, output) pairs in the \texttt{exception\_only} format (correct executions raise no exceptions, so the trace content is the same regardless of the solution's internal logic), the dataset contains duplicate rows.
Train--test input overlap is zero (split by problem ID), so no information leakage occurs.
The high duplication in \texttt{exception\_only} does not affect our experimental conclusions: after deduplication the training set still contains 2,858 unique samples and the test set 607, providing sufficient coverage for the 591-problem benchmark.

\paragraph{Problem-level partitioning and sensitivity analysis.}
Data is partitioned at the problem level: 472 training problems and 119 test problems, with zero crossover.
Duplicates arise from multiple candidate solutions per problem (up to 10 solutions each), not from cross-problem overlap.
To verify that deduplication does not alter any finding, we ran a sensitivity analysis across all 19 experimental conditions (7 trace formats $\times$ 4 models, minus conditions not run): deduplication produces a negligible ($<$0.1pp) accuracy delta in every case.
This shows that duplicate samples neither inflate nor deflate accuracy, because duplicates share the same ground-truth label and the model's prediction is deterministic at inference time.
Duplicates arise because the \texttt{exception\_only} format collapses passing solutions (which share identical ``no exception'' output) into identical rows; the redundancy is a property of the format's compactness for pass-class samples.
The \texttt{exception\_only} test set contains 48.99\% such duplicates; all confidence intervals treat samples as independent Bernoulli trials.

The SFT advantage increases with format complexity: \texttt{no\_trace} (+3.62pp over majority baseline) $<$ \texttt{full\_trace} (+4.37pp) $<$ \texttt{exception\_only} (+6.22pp) $\ll$ VOTA (+23.86pp).
The VOTA gap is largest because its structured multi-component format carries semantic content that regex cannot parse, while \texttt{exception\_only}'s simpler format allows regex to capture most of the signal.

\section{Cross-Model Zero-Shot Comparison}
\label{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}

Table~\ref{tab:zeroshot_cross_model} compares zero-shot and SFT \texttt{exception\_only} accuracy across four models.
Zero-shot performance does not correlate with model size: the smallest model (Qwen-1.5B, 93.45\%) outperforms all larger models, while the largest (CodeLlama-13B) falls below majority baseline.
SFT compresses the 42.44pp zero-shot range to 0.50pp, eliminating architecture-dependent variance.

\section{Use of AI Assistants}
\label{app:ai-assistants}

We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding and writing assistant
throughout this work. Specifically:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Code:} drafting experiment scripts, data-processing
    pipelines, and analysis utilities; debugging and refactoring.
    \item \textbf{Writing:} drafting and revising paper sections,
    polishing prose, and reformatting LaTeX.
    \item \textbf{Literature:} summarizing related papers to inform
    the related-work section.
\end{itemize}

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces (line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior) have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{liu2023codeexecution,chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,ding2024semcoder,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
The intuition is straightforward: more execution information should help the model make better predictions.
Yet for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails), this intuition is wrong.
Complete traces \emph{actively degrade} accuracy compared to compact exception events, despite containing strictly more information.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig1_trace_overview}
\vspace{-8pt}
\caption{Overview of the verdict prediction pipeline. Source code and a test input are executed to produce a full raw trace, from which four conditions extract different representations: \texttt{no\_trace} (source code only), \texttt{full\_trace} (complete line-by-line trace), VOTA (Verdict-Optimized Trace Abstraction: exception events, assertion comparisons, and loop summaries), and \texttt{exception\_only} (only exception/error events). Information density decreases from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only}, yet accuracy follows the opposite direction (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}). Appendix~\ref{sec:vota_examples} provides input/output examples.}
\label{fig:trace_overview}
\end{figure*}


Prior work found trace utility to be task-dependent \citep{wang2025dcsh}, but focused on generation-oriented tasks where output noise confounds the analysis.
Verdict prediction offers a cleaner testbed: as binary classification, it isolates the learning signal from generation noise, and controlled component ablation directly measures how trace content affects SFT learning.
This approach aligns with recent *ACL precedent: CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval} uses execution prediction to probe code reasoning, and NExT \citep{ni2024next} uses trace-augmented chain-of-thought for program repair.

We present a systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and Mostly Basic Python Problems--sanitized (MBPP-sanitized) \citep{austin2021program}, we evaluate four models across three architecture families and 1.5B to 13B parameters: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2024coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

The central result: complete traces (77--82\%) barely improve over source code alone, while compact exception events achieve near-perfect accuracy (${\geq}$99\%) across all four models, an 18--23 percentage-point (pp) gap (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
A simple regex exploiting a format marker matches this ceiling, so the interesting question is not why exceptions help but \emph{why complete traces hurt}.
Marker removal collapses the regex to near-chance while SFT retains $>$97\%; cross-dataset transfer confirms SFT acquires diagnostic patterns beyond format matching (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

Gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution; content quality at inference accounts for the majority (\S\ref{sec:density}).
Training dynamics corroborate this: \texttt{exception\_only} converges within 50 steps while \texttt{full\_trace} oscillates without convergence (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}).
A tail-truncation budget sweep reveals a sharp performance transition near 512 tokens, coinciding with the first appearance of structured execution markers (\S\ref{sec:trace_length}).

While exception events structurally encode verdict direction (exception present typically implies failure), the non-trivial finding is that providing strictly more information (complete traces containing all exception data) degrades performance by 18--23pp.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Complete traces degrade SFT verdict accuracy} despite containing all diagnostic information: across four models (1.5B--13B, three families), complete traces (77--82\%) remain near source-code-only levels while compact exception events close an 18--23pp gap to ${\geq}$99.33\% (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\item \textbf{Semantic vs.\ format-marker decomposition}: marker removal collapses a format-exploiting regex by 71pp while SFT drops only 2pp; cross-dataset transfer (99.4--100\%) shows the learned signal generalizes beyond format markers (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}).

\item \textbf{A two-tier signal hierarchy and its mechanistic explanation}: exception/assertion signals (${\geq}$98.53\%) dominate loop compression (77--86\%) by 12+pp with non-overlapping CIs, and a sharp transition at ${\sim}$512 tail tokens yields a practical fallback (\S\ref{sec:ablation}, \S\ref{sec:trace_length}). Controlled gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% of the degradation to gradient dilution, assigning the majority to content quality at inference (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Execution Traces for Code Large Language Models (LLMs).}
TracePile \citep{chen2025tracepile} scaled trace-augmented training to 2.6M samples; \citet{wang2025dcsh} found trace utility task- and format-dependent, which we extend by showing that complete traces degrade SFT performance while compact exception events suffice.
Earlier, \citet{liu2023codeexecution} pre-trained on execution prediction, SemCoder \citep{ding2024semcoder} introduced monologue reasoning to link code with runtime states, and \citet{dimenna2025execution} studied execution-aware models for code optimization.
NExT \citep{ni2024next} and ET-CoT \citep{eguchi2025etcot} used trace chain-of-thought for repair and execution reasoning; \citet{ferrando2025execute} found compact traces comparable to full traces, and \citet{haque2025traces} showed trace utility for repair diminishes with complexity, both supporting our density finding.
CRUXEval \citep{gu2024cruxeval,xu2025cruxevalx} and LiveCodeBench \citep{jain2024livecodebench} established execution reasoning benchmarks, but none decompose which trace components contribute to classification accuracy.

\paragraph{Verdict Prediction and Fault Localization.}
TRACED \citep{ding2024traced} showed execution-aware pretraining improves vulnerability detection; CC2Vec \citep{hoang2020cc2vec}, APPT \citep{appt2024}, and LLM-based patch assessment \citep{zhou2024llm4patch} developed representation learning and evaluation of code changes, extending just-in-time quality assurance \citep{kamei2013large}; verdict prediction is an instance of the test oracle problem \citep{barr2015oracle,bodicoat2026oracle}.
Spectrum-based fault localization (SBFL; \citealp{jones2002visualization,abreu2007accuracy,wong2014dstar}) and LLM-based fault localization \citep{kang2024autofl,qin2024agentfl,shi2025farloc} share our insight that anomalous execution events carry the strongest diagnostic signal, though LLM fault localizability remains fragile under semantic-preserving mutations \citep{haroon2026faultlocalizability}.
TraceCoder \citep{huang2026tracecoder} and InspectCoder \citep{wang2025inspectcoder} use selective trace extraction, and LLM repair agents \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent,xia2024agentless,bouzenia2025repairagent,wang2025openhands} increasingly leverage execution feedback, yet which trace components carry verdict signals most efficiently remains unstudied.

\paragraph{Calibration and Data Selection.}
Neural network calibration \citep{guo2017calibration}, extended to LLMs \citep{kadavath2022language,geng2024calibration,liu2025uqsurvey}, studies confidence-correctness alignment; our Expected Calibration Error (ECE) ${<}$ 0.007 suggests compact inputs improve calibration.
The Information Bottleneck \citep{tishby2000information}, feature selection theory \citep{guyon2003introduction}, IB-guided code fine-tuning \citep{wang2025ibft}, and LIMA \citep{zhou2023lima} predict that compressing task-irrelevant information improves learning; data pruning \citep{paul2021deep,sorscher2022beyond}, curriculum learning \citep{bengio2009curriculum}, and data-efficient code SFT \citep{lv2025dataefficient,shang2025thtb} confirm this empirically, consistent with our finding that compact exceptions converge rapidly while verbose traces oscillate.
Prompt compression methods \citep{jiang2023llmlingua,li2023selectivecontext} pursue a complementary goal at inference time.
